text: This looks like a video.
It isn't. That cursor? A viewer — dragging the molecule, spinning the camera. In a Flow Video, the lesson is alive.
Got a question? Ask it. Out loud.
Not the internet. This. Video.
When the story hits a fork? Your viewers choose. They don't watch it — they steer it.
On a phone, it stays vertical — the frame follows your speaker. And the same video? It speaks Spanish.
Making one? Upload your video. Drop in a simulation — no code. Tell the AI what your viewers can touch. Share one link. That's a Flow Video.
Don't take my word for it. The next section of this timeline is live. Go scatter the flock.
Touch it. Ask it. Steer it. — Flow Video.
You just met a living simulation. Here's the whole build — start to share — in the next two minutes.
New project, name it, create. Your Library's on the right, timeline below. Drop everything in at once — footage, images, audio, even a whole simulation as a zip. It sorts itself.
Your video sits on V-one. Now the move that changes everything: drag across the moment you want to come alive. That marks a section.

Pick Simulation, choose your package. This Orbit Lab came in with that drop — a real gravity sandbox, and it's just a file. No code. Now tell it what this moment is for: type what your viewer should see and touch. Flip on Simple UI — it hides every control that doesn't matter. Flip on Auto Script — it animates the demonstration for viewers who just watch. Hit Generate with AI.
Watch the Preview: the AI wired your simulation to this exact moment. Viewers get just the controls you chose — nothing else in their way.
Layer it up: b-roll on V-two — generate it from a prompt if you don't have footage. Music on A-two. Images with camera moves. And "Follow user decisions" branches the story on your viewers' choices.

Settings finishes it: generate your title and thumbnail with AI. Give the video an avatar your viewers can question. Smart Crop keeps phones upright — the frame follows your speaker. Then decide who can watch. Done.
Hit Share. Pick your address. That one link is the whole experience — the interactive video, a podcast version that answers voice questions, even your asset library as its own page.

And this project — the one you're inside right now — was built exactly this way. That Orbit Lab below? You just watched it get built. It's yours now: change one word of the prompt, hit Generate, and watch it obey. Then ship your own.
Some simulations are heavy. Thirty megabytes of three-D models and live code heavy. Watch how Flow Video treats one.
Zip it. Drop it. That's the whole import. No size police, no special format — your files, exactly as you built them.
Mark the moment, tell it what it's for — and here's the part that matters for big sims: Simple UI. Seven controls become two. Your viewer sees exactly what you chose, and nothing else.
Don't like the first cut? Say so — in English. "Make the timeline bigger. Hide the background toggle." The AI remembers the conversation and rewires it.
And when your video reaches this moment? The simulation is already warm. Poster first, then the live thing — fully loaded, sixty frames a second. No spinners. Not ever. That's the rule.
Big science. Small controls. Smooth as glass. Drop yours in — the editor does the heavy lifting.
Your viewers have powers here. Four of them. Count along.
One: touch. Any simulation section is live. Launch a planet — watch the forces pull it into orbit.
Two: ask. Out loud, mid-video. Listen.
Grounded in this lesson. Not the internet.
Three: choose. The story pauses, your viewer picks a path, and the video follows their decision.
Four: watch it their way. Vertical on phones — the frame follows the speaker. Another language? Same video, same voice, dubbed. And captions ride along everywhere.
Touch, ask, choose, their way. Give your viewers powers — they'll give you their attention. That's a Flow Video.
You built it. Let's ship it — one link, three doors.
Hit Create link. Your video gets a public page. Same link, slash audio — a podcast that answers voice questions. Slash library — every asset, browsable.
Want it memorable? Pick your own address and publish there. That's the link you put on a slide, in a bio, on a syllabus.
Working with a team? Invite collaborators — they edit, you stay the owner. And Access decides who watches: everyone, anyone holding your link — or just you.
Viewers need nothing — no app, no account, no download. The link is the product: interactive on day one, on any screen.
Build once. Share one link. Teach everywhere.
Why does it move in eight-nanometer steps?
Why doesn't the moon crash into the earth?
